questions.question: An agent makes four model calls of about 0.25s each. Roughly how long do they take sequentially versus concurrently?
questions.explanation: Sequential is the sum of the waits. Concurrent is about as long as the slowest single call, because the waits overlap.

questions.question: Where should untrusted JSON from a model or tool be validated?
options: Wherever a field is first used
Once, at the boundary where it enters the program, turning it into typed objects
It doesn't need validation if it came from your own API call
questions.explanation: Validate once at the boundary. Everything past that point can trust the types; scattered checks miss cases.

questions.question: Why wrap each call in asyncio.wait_for(..., timeout)?
options: So one hung call becomes an error result instead of freezing the whole agent
questions.explanation: Without a per-call timeout, gather waits for the slowest call forever. The timeout turns a hang into a reportable failure.

questions.question: In what order does asyncio.gather return results?
options: The order the awaitables were passed in
questions.explanation: gather preserves input order, which is what lets you map results back to the tool calls that produced them.

questions.question: You fire 200 tool calls at once with gather and no limit. What's the most likely problem?
options: Rate limits (429s) from the provider, or a local server queueing and timing out, so you need a semaphore
The results come back in the wrong order
questions.explanation: Async makes unbounded fan-out easy, but providers and servers have limits. A semaphore caps calls in flight.

questions.question: Why does main.ts avoid TypeScript enums?
options: Node's built-in TypeScript support only strips erasable syntax; enums generate runtime code and need a compiler
questions.explanation: Type stripping deletes type annotations. Enums and parameter properties emit JavaScript, so they'd need a build step.
